If you're picturing your own retirement decades down the road or helping a parent or grandparent who is living on just Social Security , it's natural to wonder how benefits change as recipients age into their 90s. Does Social Security pay more the longer you live? Does one birthday suddenly bump up your check? The Social Security Administration (SSA) actually tracks average benefit amounts by age, and the numbers for 92-year-olds tell a more nuanced story than you might expect. Here's what the data shows, and why your own benefit may land somewhere very different. Read More Here › SPONSORED The average benefit for 92-year-olds, according to the SSA According to the SSA's Office of the Chief Actuary, which tracks retired-worker beneficiaries in current payment status by age and sex, the average monthly benefit among 92-year-old retired workers was $1,899.20 as of the end of December 2025. That figure covers 266,739 retired workers at that age. It's worth being precise about what this number includes. The SSA's age-breakdown table covers retired-worker beneficiaries only. It excludes people receiving survivor benefits, spousal benefits, or disability benefits, so it's not a picture of "everyone age 92 who gets a Social Security check." It's specifically retirees drawing benefits on their own earnings record (or, in some cases, a blended benefit tied to dual entitlement, explained below). Because this is a December 2025 snapshot, it reflects benefit amounts before the 2.8% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) that took effect for payments starting in January 2026, according to the SSA's 2026 COLA fact sheet. The SSA has not yet published a separate age-by-age breakdown reflecting the new COLA. If you wanted to estimate what a comparable 92-year-old's benefit might look like after the adjustment, you could apply the 2.8% increase to the December 2025 average as rough math, landing somewhere near $1,952.  But that's an estimate based on a flat percentage adjustment, not a separately measured figure, since COLAs apply to each individual's benefit rather than to a population average uniformly. Average Social Security benefits at age 92 for men and women The SSA's data also splits this figure by sex, and the gap is notable. Among 92-year-olds, men received an average of $1,986.52 per month, while women received an average of $1,835.01, as of December 2025. That roughly $151 monthly gap mirrors a pattern that shows up across nearly every age group in the SSA's retired-worker data, not just among 92-year-olds. It traces back largely to lifetime earnings differences. Social Security benefits are calculated from a worker's average indexed monthly earnings (AIME), based on up to 35 years of wage-indexed earnings. Workers with higher lifetime earnings, more years in the workforce, or longer uninterrupted careers generally end up with a higher benefit, regardless of age. Women in this generation were more likely to have taken time out of paid work for caregiving or to have earned less over their careers than men, which can translate into a lower retired-worker benefit decades later. It's also worth noting that many women in their 90s receive a dually entitled benefit, meaning their payment combines their own work record with a higher amount available through a spouse's record. The SSA's data shows that among 92-year-olds specifically, those who are not dually entitled average $1,844.38, while dually entitled retired workers average $1,992.92 in the same month. Why age alone doesn't drive the benefit amount higher It's tempting to assume that reaching 92 means decades of COLAs have stacked up into a bigger check than younger retirees receive. The data doesn't fully support that assumption. Looking at the SSA's age-by-age table for December 2025, the average benefit generally peaks somewhere in the late 60s to low 70s, then gradually declines through the 80s and 90s: 67-year-olds averaged $2,016.48, 70-year-olds averaged $2,274.68, and by 92, the average had fallen to $1,899.20. Several factors explain this pattern. COLAs do increase benefits annually, but the base benefit for someone who claimed decades ago, when average wages (and therefore benefit calculations) were lower, often started smaller than what a worker retiring today receives. Newer retirees also tend to have higher lifetime earnings on record, reflecting decades of wage growth, so each new cohort entering the data can push up the averages for people in their late 60s and 70s relative to those who claimed benefits much earlier. In short, a benefit amount is locked in largely by earnings history and the age at which someone claimed, and COLAs adjust that starting point. Living longer doesn't reset or boost the underlying calculation. Learn More Here › SPONSORED How your claiming age and work history affect your Social Security benefits Two factors made decades before someone turns 92 do most of the work in determining their benefit: how much they earned and when they claimed. The SSA calculates retirement benefits using a worker's highest 35 years of wage-indexed earnings. Claiming before full retirement age (FRA), which is 67 for people born in 1960 or later, permanently reduces the monthly benefit. Claiming after FRA, up to age 70, increases it through delayed retirement credits, worth roughly 8% per year, according to the SSA.  For 2026, the SSA states that a worker who claims at age 62 could receive a benefit around $2,969 per month, while someone claiming at full retirement age could receive around $4,152, and someone who waits until age 70 could receive as much as $5,181 per month, the maximum payable to a new retiree this year. That $5,181 figure assumes the worker earned at or above the taxable maximum (Social Security's capped earnings subject to tax, $184,500 for 2026) in every one of roughly 35 working years, not simply that they worked that long. Someone who is 92 today claimed benefits decades ago, under different wage levels, different bend-point formulas, and possibly very different personal circumstances. That history, not their current age, is what mostly explains why their check may be smaller or larger than a 65- or 70-year-old's today. How to compare your Social Security benefit with the average For context, the SSA's 2026 COLA fact sheet estimates the average monthly benefit for all retired workers, across every age, at $2,071 starting in January 2026, after the 2.8% COLA. That's noticeably higher than the December 2025 average for 92-year-olds specifically, underscoring that age group averages can look quite different from the overall population average. Anyone who wants to know how their own benefit compares can use the SSA's online my Social Security account to view a personalized earnings record and estimated benefit at different claiming ages, which is a more accurate comparison than any population average. Bottom line The average Social Security benefit among 92-year-old retired workers was $1,899.20 per month as of December 2025, according to the SSA, with men averaging $1,986.52 and women averaging $1,835.01. That gap, and the overall below-average figure for this age group, traces back mostly to lifetime earnings and claiming-age decisions made years earlier, not to any automatic increase tied to reaching a particular age. Whatever the benefit amount, Social Security is designed to continue for as long as someone lives, with annual COLAs intended to help it keep pace with inflation. That durability, not the size of any single age group's average, is often the more meaningful number to focus on when trying to stretch your retirement dollars further .   FAQs Does Social Security increase with age? No automatic increase comes with any age. Benefits can rise through cost-of-living adjustments, but reaching a particular birthday does not trigger an extra payment. Delayed retirement credits stop accumulating at age 70. Can someone in their 90s qualify for benefits through a spouse's work record? Yes. An eligible older adult may qualify for spousal or survivor benefits based on a spouse's work record. If they also qualify for their own retirement benefit, Social Security coordinates the payments rather than paying both full benefits together. What other sources of income might a 90-year-old have besides Social Security? Other sources may include pension payments, withdrawals from IRAs or 401(k)s, interest from savings accounts and CDs, investment dividends, and rental income. Some older adults also receive financial support from family. The mix varies widely, and not everyone has substantial income beyond Social Security.
